paras: The lynching of Cleveland McBee was the hanging and shooting of a Black youth by a mob at Cedar Bluff, Mississippi, in late August 1905. McBee was accused of assaulting the twelve-year-old daughter of a farmer on whose place he lived, and the mob cut the railroad wires so that the Governor would not learn of the killing. The only report found is a front-page story in the Columbus Dispatch, which presented the hanging as a deserved penalty.

Cedar Bluff was described as a small station on the Southern Railway west of Columbus, between West Point and Winona. According to the Dispatch, on the morning of Thursday, August 24, at about eight o'clock, the young daughter of Jack Thomas, a farmer living twelve miles from Cedar Bluff, was assaulted and injured by a "negro boy on the place."

The accused was captured within moments, and Thomas locked him in his barn under his son's guard while he went to Cedar Bluff for physicians. The paper named the prisoner as Cleveland McBee and said he was then carried to Cedar Bluff, where a mob gathered. There, in the Dispatch's words, he was "very quietly and very orderly hung and his body riddled with bullets." The mob also cut the railroad wires so that "the outside world, including the Governor," would not know what was happening.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any response from the Governor appears in the coverage.

The Columbus Dispatch ran the story on August 31 under the headline "Paid the Penalty with His Life" and the deck "Negro Brute at Cedar Bluff, Mississippi, Hung by a Mob For the Usual Crime." The paper stated the accusation as fact, calling it a "fiendish and atrocious crime," and stressed the mob's orderliness rather than the absence of a trial. No other white paper and no Black paper in the coverage is known to have reported the Cedar Bluff hanging; a lynching at Rosetta, Mississippi, carried by wire in the first days of September, involved a different man, place and charge.

reader.title: Lynching of Cleveland McBee
bases: The Columbus Dispatch reports that a mob hanged an accused Black youth at Cedar Bluff and riddled his body with bullets (A1, A2).

A mob hanged Cleveland McBee and shot his body after he was accused of assaulting a farmer's daughter, with no legal process reported, and cut the telegraph wires to keep the Governor from learning of it (A1, A2). The mob's size is not given, but the paper calls it a 'mob' that 'gathered' (A2).
The only report found is a single Columbus Dispatch article printed in two pieces on one page (A1, A2); the Rosetta wire items of Sept. 1-9 describe a different lynching (A3, A4).

accounts.label: Columbus Dispatch local report
accounts.gist: Presents the assault as fact and McBee as a 'brute'; says he was captured within moments, held in a barn, carried to Cedar Bluff and hanged and shot by a mob that cut the railroad wires.

framing.detail: The Columbus Dispatch headlined 'PAID THE PENALTY WITH HIS LIFE' and 'Negro Brute ... Hung by a Mob For the Usual Crime', called the alleged assault 'fiendish and atrocious', and described the hanging as 'very quietly and very orderly'.

Cedar Bluff, 'a small station on the line of the Southern Railway west of Columbus and between West Point and Winona'; the Thomas farm was twelve miles from Cedar Bluff.
Cleveland McBee, described as a 'negro boy on the place' (the Thomas farm).
Accused of assaulting and injuring the twelve-year-old daughter of Jack Thomas, a farmer.
